pl-l3d16c1-d1e117.summary: Raises a question arising from what was said: Christ took our defects except sin, and there is a general human defect that is not sin, the necessity of suffering or dying; hence our body is called not only mortal but dead, having not only the aptitude but the necessity of dying. Was such necessity in Christ's body?
claims: The necessity of dying is a general defect that is not sin.

pl-l3d16c1-d1e120.summary: States that the aptitude for dying was certainly in him; it was in man before sin, when there was no defect in him, so that mortality was no defect, being natural to him. Some therefore rightly say that such mortality is not a defect in us, but the necessity of dying or suffering, also called mortality or passibility; man is now called passible or mortal not only for aptitude but for necessity.
claims: The aptitude for dying is not a defect.
The necessity of dying is the defect.

pl-l3d16c1-d1e123.summary: Sharpens the question: was this defect in Christ's flesh? Did his soul, passible before death, have the necessity of suffering? If so, he does not seem to have taken our defects by mercy's will alone.

pl-l3d16c1-d1e127.summary: Answers that Christ took these defects, like the others, by will and not by necessity of his nature: the necessity of suffering in soul, and of suffering and dying in flesh.
claims: Christ took the necessity of suffering and dying by will.

pl-l3d16c1-d1e130.summary: Adds that he did not have this necessity by necessity of his condition, being free from sin, but took it from our weakness by will alone, placing his tabernacle in the sun (Ps 18:6), i.e., under temporal change and toil.
claims: Christ's necessity of dying did not arise from his sinless condition.

pl-l3d16c1-d1e136.summary: Interprets the gloss on Hebrews: as other men are appointed to die once by right and law of nature, so Christ was offered once by the same necessity and law of nature. 'Law of nature' does not mean he contracted this defect from his nature; it does not come to us from nature as first instituted but as vitiated by sin. It is called a natural defect because it has grown in like a nature, spread through all.
claims: The necessity of death comes from nature vitiated by sin, not nature as created.
It is called natural because it is universal, like a second nature.

pl-l3d16c1.summary: Asks whether the necessity of suffering and dying, a general human defect that is not sin, was in Christ's body. The aptitude for dying was in him, as it was in man before sin, when it was no defect; the necessity of dying is the defect. Christ took the necessity of suffering in soul and of suffering and dying in flesh by will, not by necessity of his sinless condition. The gloss on Hebrews saying he died once 'by law of nature' means nature as vitiated by sin, a defect called natural because it spread to all like a second nature.
claims: Christ had the aptitude for dying, which was no defect even before sin.
The necessity of dying is a defect of fallen nature.
Christ took the necessity of suffering and dying by will, not by condition.
This defect is called natural because it has become like a second nature in all.
